query: Consider the following context: During the hot dip aluminum plating process, components such as sinking rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates will come into long-term contact with high-temperature liquid aluminum and be corroded by the aluminum liquid, greatly reducing their service life. In that context, which material can be used for prepare parts for the dipping and plating equipment and protect the equipment from erosion, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) component, when coated with a silicide-based diffusion barrier, will exhibit significantly enhanced resistance to molten aluminum erosion compared to uncoated RHEA components.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., an equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy in its high-temperature stable phase) without any protective coating.
generation.intervention: Apply a silicide-based diffusion barrier coating (via pack cementation or a similar surface treatment) on the RHEA component.
generation.conditions: Components are exposed to high-temperature molten aluminum under conditions similar to those in a hot-dip aluminum plating process (continuous or prolonged immersion at temperatures above aluminum’s melting point).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a dense, stable silicide layer on the RHEA substrate.
generation.mechanism: The silicide layer acts as a diffusion barrier that limits the direct contact and chemical interaction between the molten aluminum and the refractory alloy substrate, thereby reducing corrosion and erosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Silicide-coated RHEA components will have lower weight loss and display less surface degradation after prolonged exposure to molten aluminum compared to uncoated RHEA components or conventional materials.
generation.baseline: Performance of standard uncoated RHEA components or conventional materials (e.g., untreated steels) under identical molten aluminum exposure conditions.
generation.boundary: The protective effect may diminish if the silicide coating degrades or delaminates over extremely long exposures or under severe thermal cycling; optimal coating uniformity and integrity are critical.
generation.uncertainty: While positive effects are anticipated based on analogous high-temperature oxidation studies, the long-term stability and precise performance improvement of the silicide coating in direct molten aluminum environments remain to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of RHEA components: one set with the silicide-based coating and one set without. Immerse both sets in molten aluminum at industry-relevant temperatures for an extended period that mimics operational exposure. Periodically measure weight loss, inspect the surface morphology (using microscopic techniques), and analyze phase compositions.
measurements: Surface morphology changes via scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
Phase composition and coating integrity via X-ray diffraction (XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the silicide-coated components do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in weight loss and surface degradation compared to the uncoated components, or if the silicide layer exhibits rapid degradation/disruption under test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. Abstract An oxygen‐resistant refractory high‐entropy alloy is synthesized in microlattice or bulk form by 3D ink‐extrusion printing, interdiffusion, and silicide coating. Additive manufacturing of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr is implemented by extruding inks containing hydride powders, de‐binding under H 2 , and sintering under vacuum. The sequential decomposition of hydride powders (HfH 2 +NbH+TaH 0.5 +TiH 2 +ZrH 2 ) is followed by in situ X‐ray diffraction. Upon sintering at 1400 °C for 18 h, a nearly fully densified, equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy is synthesized; on slow cooling, both α‐HCP and β‐BCC phases are formed, but on quenching, a metastable single β‐BCC phase is obtained. Printed and sintered HfNbTaTiZr alloys with ≈1 wt.% O shows excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures. Oxidation resistance is achieved by silicide coating via pack cementation. A small‐size lattice‐core sandwich is fabricated and tested with high‐temperature flames to demonstrate the versatility of this sequential approach (printing, sintering, and siliconizing) for high‐temperature, high‐stress applications of refractory high‐entropy alloys. Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

decision.trend: Studies on refractory and high-entropy alloys under molten or high-temperature conditions (as in PMC6908586 for FLiBe, PMC10142552 for W-based coatings, and PMC11077685 for silicide-coated RHEAs) show that specialized alloys and protective surface layers can outperform conventional steels and superalloys. Research has progressed from exploring corrosion in molten salts to developing refractory high-entropy alloy coatings via laser cladding or pack cementation, improving high-temperature stability and oxidation resistance. However, few detailed data exist for molten aluminum contact, and the long-term stability of these materials under direct aluminum attack remains insufficiently explored.
decision.unsolved: While refractory high-entropy alloys and their coatings have demonstrated promising thermal stability, oxidation resistance, and reduced corrosion in other aggressive environments, their long-term corrosion and erosion performance in molten aluminum needs further study. Achieving robust, durable, and cost-effective protection for rollers and guide plates requires more targeted research on stable surface layers that can resist dissolution and reaction with liquid aluminum.
decision.lever: Apply a silicide-based diffusion barrier coating to a refractory high-entropy alloy component
decision.why: Building on the refractory alloys’ high-temperature integrity, adding a silicide coating by pack cementation or a similar route can form a stable, protective layer against molten aluminum. This approach aligns with prior success in high-temperature oxidation and corrosion scenarios and addresses the specialized challenge of aluminum-induced erosion.
